title: Systems & Hardware Languages
summary: C, C++, Rust, Go, Zig, assembly and hardware description languages: close to the machine, where you choose the memory layout and pay for every abstraction. Rust's ownership model is the threshold of this family.
sources: Kernighan & Ritchie: The C Programming Language
Klabnik & Nichols: The Rust Programming Language
Donovan & Kernighan: The Go Programming Language
Harris & Harris: Digital Design and Computer Architecture

nodes.label: C: Pointers & Memory
nodes.summary: Addresses, arrays and manual allocation with malloc and free.
nodes.outcome: Trace pointer arithmetic and manage heap memory in C.
nodes.check: In C, what does *p mean when p is a pointer?
nodes.answer: Dereference: the value stored at the address p holds.

nodes.label: C: Undefined Behaviour
nodes.summary: Out-of-bounds access, signed overflow and use-after-free let the compiler do anything.
nodes.outcome: Spot undefined behaviour and enable sanitizers to catch it.
nodes.check: What may a C compiler do with code that reads past the end of an array?
nodes.answer: Anything: it is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it never happens, and results are unpredictable.

nodes.label: C++: RAII & Destructors
nodes.summary: Resources tied to object lifetimes: acquired in constructors, released in destructors.
nodes.outcome: Write a RAII wrapper and use smart pointers.
nodes.check: In C++ RAII, when is a resource such as a file or lock released?
nodes.answer: Automatically in the destructor, when the owning object goes out of scope.

nodes.label: C++: Templates & the STL
nodes.summary: Generic containers and algorithms with zero-cost abstraction.
nodes.outcome: Choose STL containers and algorithms for a task.
nodes.check: What does std::vector<int> give you that a raw C array doesn't?
nodes.answer: It manages its own memory, grows automatically and knows its size.

nodes.label: Rust: Ownership & Borrowing
nodes.summary: Each value has one owner; references are borrowed under rules the compiler checks, ruling out data races and use-after-free. Troublesome because the compiler rejects code that 'looks fine'.
nodes.outcome: Fix borrow-checker errors by restructuring ownership.
nodes.check: In Rust, how many mutable references to a value may exist at the same time?
nodes.answer: One, and no immutable references alongside it: this rule prevents data races at compile time.

nodes.label: "Rust programs can never crash"
nodes.summary: Rust prevents memory-safety bugs, not all failures: out-of-bounds indexing and unwrap on None still panic.
nodes.outcome: Handle errors with Result instead of panicking.
nodes.check: Can a safe Rust program still panic?
nodes.answer: Yes: indexing out of bounds or calling unwrap on None panics; Rust prevents memory-safety bugs, not every failure.

nodes.label: Go: Goroutines & Simplicity
nodes.summary: A small language with built-in concurrency, fast compiles and a garbage collector.
nodes.outcome: Write a concurrent Go program with goroutines and channels.
nodes.check: How do you run a function concurrently in Go?
nodes.answer: Prefix the call with the go keyword: go f().

nodes.label: Zig: Explicit Allocation
nodes.summary: No hidden control flow or allocations; comptime replaces macros.
nodes.check: How does Zig make memory allocation explicit?
nodes.answer: Functions that allocate take an allocator parameter, so every allocation is visible at the call site.

nodes.label: Assembly
nodes.summary: Mnemonics for machine instructions: registers, jumps and the stack.
nodes.outcome: Read the assembly a compiler produces for a small function.
nodes.check: What does an assembler translate, and into what?
nodes.answer: Human-readable mnemonics (like MOV and ADD) into machine-code bytes, almost one to one.

nodes.label: Verilog & VHDL: Describing Hardware
nodes.summary: Hardware description languages describe circuits that synthesise to gates on FPGAs and chips.
nodes.outcome: Describe a counter in Verilog and simulate it.
nodes.check: How does a hardware description language differ from a programming language like C?
nodes.answer: It describes circuits whose parts all operate in parallel, not a sequence of instructions executed one after another.

nodes.label: "An HDL program runs line by line"
nodes.summary: Always blocks triggered by the same clock edge describe hardware that updates simultaneously.
nodes.outcome: Reason about simultaneous updates on a clock edge.
nodes.check: In Verilog, two always blocks both trigger on the same clock edge. Which runs first?
nodes.answer: Neither: they describe hardware that updates in parallel on that edge.
